description:
The Colonna Palace sits at the base of the Quirinal Hill, its back gardens rising on terraces toward the presidential palace above. The family that owns it — the Colonnas — has held this position since the early 14th century, making the Palazzo Colonna the oldest continuously inhabited private palace in Rome: not oldest by construction date, but oldest by unbroken family occupation, an institutional continuity that no public Roman museum can claim.

The current palace is not the 14th-century structure. What the Colonnas held for centuries was rebuilt wholesale beginning in the mid-1600s, when Cardinal Girolamo I Colonna commissioned the Great Gallery and his nephew Lorenzo Onofrio Colonna extended the project into the largest private palace complex in Rome. The rebuilding was the most ambitious private architectural undertaking in 17th-century Rome: a palace that would house the family's art collection in interiors of palatial grandeur, with a garden rising from the courtyard up the Quirinal Hill behind.

The Great Gallery (Grande Galleria) is what the palace was built to contain. Approximately 76 metres long, colonnaded, its yellow marble columns giving the room — and the family — their heraldic colour, the gallery's painted vaulted ceiling carries allegorical frescoes celebrating the Battle of Lepanto (1571). At Lepanto, Marco Antonio II Colonna commanded the papal fleet that, alongside the Spanish and Venetian navies, defeated the Ottoman fleet in the decisive naval engagement of the 16th-century Mediterranean; the Battle of Lepanto prevented Ottoman naval domination of the western Mediterranean, and it made Marco Antonio Colonna a figure of European historical significance. The ceiling frescoes, painted by Giovanni Coli and Filippo Gherardi in the 1670s–80s, place this Colonna victory at the centre of an allegorical programme in which the family's heraldic column (colonna = column) and its naval triumph structure the entire decorative logic of the room.

The walls of the gallery are hung with works by Bronzino, Guercino, Tintoretto, Salvator Rosa, Francesco Salviati, and Guido Reni, alongside the family portrait cycle that documents the Colonna lineage across 17th and 18th centuries in an unbroken visual record. The accumulative hang — paintings on every available wall surface, frames touching frames — is the historic convention, unmodified by modern curatorial distance.

At the top of the staircase leading to the gallery, a French cannonball from the 1849 bombardment of Rome remains embedded in the marble steps. The Colonna family chose to leave it where it fell, preserving the scar rather than repairing it. It is the gallery's most effective single historical object — more immediate in communicating what it means for a building to have a continuous history than any painting.

The gallery's traditional opening pattern of Saturday mornings only (09:00–13:15) is the most significant practical constraint for visitors. This is not a curatorial choice but a structural feature of a palace that continues to function as a private aristocratic residence. The GYG entry ticket (t440527, from $36, with guided tour included as standard) is the most reliable way to secure entry with advance confirmation. The optional Princess Isabelle apartments upgrade extends the visit into rooms furnished for a 19th-century Colonna who was one of Rome's most significant women antiquarians, with additional collecting history not visible on the standard tour.

4.8★ across 878 reviews — the gallery's top-rated badge on GYG reflects both the quality of the collection and the distinctive experience of visiting a working private palace on Saturday mornings in Rome.

[Palazzo Doria Pamphilj](/castles/italy/palazzo-doria-pamphilj) — Rome's other great private gallery, a short walk west on Via del Corso, with the Velázquez portrait of Innocent X and two early Caravaggios — is the essential companion visit. [Castel Sant'Angelo](/castles/italy/castel-santangelo) and [Palazzo Venezia](/castles/italy/palazzo-venezia) complete the central Rome historic palace circuit.
history: 14th century: Colonna family establishes their principal Roman residence at the base of the Quirinal Hill; medieval tower and buildings on the current site. 1417: election of Oddone Colonna as Pope Martin V; the Colonna family reaches the height of its ecclesiastical and political power; first significant palace improvements. 1571: Battle of Lepanto; Marco Antonio II Colonna commands the papal fleet; the victory becomes the defining event in the Colonna family's self-presentation. Mid-1600s: Cardinal Girolamo I Colonna commissions the Great Gallery (Grande Galleria); construction and decoration begin. 1670s–1680s: Giovanni Coli and Filippo Gherardi paint the Lepanto ceiling frescoes in the Great Gallery. Late 17th century: Lorenzo Onofrio Colonna extends the palace to its current scale; gardens on the Quirinal Hill terraces developed. 1700s–1800s: continued Colonna family ownership; art collection expanded; Princess Isabelle Colonna furnishes her apartments. 1849: French cannonball strikes the palace staircase during the bombardment of the Roman Republic; left embedded in the marble as a permanent record. Present day: Galleria Colonna open Saturday mornings; Colonna family continues in private residence.
how_to_visit:
**GYG entry ticket with guided tour (~$36/person, t440527, valid 1 day):** Official Galleria Colonna entry ticket including a guided tour of the Great Gallery, the Lepanto ceiling frescoes, the cannonball room, and the principal collections. Top Rated badge on GYG. Optional upgrade: Princess Isabelle apartments guided tour. 4.8★ / 878 reviews → is_top_pick: true.

**IMPORTANT — opening schedule:** The Galleria Colonna is traditionally open on Saturday mornings only (09:00–13:15, last entry 12:45). Confirm current opening days at galleriacolonna.it before planning your visit — additional days are occasionally offered, but Saturday morning remains the primary access window.

**Getting there:** The palace is at Piazza Santi Apostoli 66, a 10-minute walk from the Trevi Fountain and 15 minutes from Piazza Venezia. Nearest metro: Barberini (5 minutes on foot).

**Visiting in context:** Combine with Palazzo Doria Pamphilj (500m west on Via del Corso — Rome's other great private gallery, open daily, with the Velázquez portrait of Innocent X) for a full Roman private noble gallery day. Both palaces together give the most complete picture of Roman aristocratic art collecting across the 17th–18th centuries.

faqs.question: Why is the Colonna Palace only open on Saturday mornings?
faqs.answer: The Galleria Colonna is open on limited days — traditionally Saturday mornings from 09:00 to 13:15 — because the Palazzo Colonna continues to function as a private aristocratic residence. The Colonna family has chosen to open the gallery on specific days rather than converting the palace to a full public museum, maintaining the private character that gives the visit its distinctive quality. The limited opening is not a curatorial decision but a structural feature of a working private palace. Confirm current opening days at galleriacolonna.it before planning your visit, as the schedule can include additional days beyond the standard Saturday morning opening.

faqs.question: What is the significance of the cannonball in the staircase?
faqs.answer: A French cannonball from the 1849 bombardment of Rome is still embedded in the marble steps at the top of the staircase leading to the Galleria Colonna. In 1849, French troops besieging the short-lived Roman Republic bombarded the city; a cannonball struck the palace staircase. The Colonna family chose to leave it in place rather than repair the damage, creating a permanent physical record of the event in the building's fabric. The cannonball is pointed out on every guided tour and functions as the gallery's most effective single historical object — more immediately communicating what it means for a building to have a continuous history than any of the paintings.

faqs.question: What does the optional Princess Isabelle apartments upgrade include?
faqs.answer: The Princess Isabelle apartments upgrade extends the standard Galleria Colonna visit into rooms furnished by Princess Isabelle Colonna, a 19th-century member of the family who was one of the significant women antiquarians and collectors of her generation in Rome. The apartments contain furniture, objects, and collecting contexts not visible on the standard tour, adding an additional layer of the Colonna family's cultural history beyond the 17th-century Great Gallery rooms. The upgrade is available at booking through the GYG entry ticket (t440527).
